This change tightens the proof that lets the translator retire an object when its frame ends: an object whose only callee is a native method (Thread.start) is no longer retired early, because the root scan then read a live Thread as freed and the sweep finalized it. Fewer objects are retired early, so peak RAM can only rise, and hello is the one workload small enough for that to show. On this CPU the result is bimodal, as on the Intel Windows x64 runner: runs for 3d3119ed9d and 95738c7ece gave medians 1.216 and 1.092, and the run for 8ac2f37307 gave rounds 1.16 0.74 0.81 0.80 0.87 (median 0.81) against the 1.154 recorded from the first two. The baseline is the middle of the three run medians, 1.092, and the memory tolerance is 0.35, as hello's RAM on the Intel Windows x64 and the Windows arm64 runners already has; it covers 0.71 to 1.47. Timing is kept.

Not a change in the translator: on this runner its self-translation time comes out in two groups, about 0.79 and about 0.58, and a run's median is whichever group three of its five rounds fell in. Runs for 3d3119ed9d (rounds 0.79 0.82 0.79 0.52 0.58, median 0.79) and 95738c7ece (0.66 0.61 0.59 0.56 0.85, median 0.61) are the same code as far as the translator goes. The baseline of 0.78 sat on the upper group, so the lower one read as an improvement past tolerance; taken from both runs it sits between them. Tolerance is kept.

The translator retires fewer objects when their frame ends, so hello's peak RAM rises, as on the other runners. On this Intel Family 6 Model 207 runner it is bimodal: two runs of this branch gave rounds 1.13 1.11 1.13 0.73 0.98 (median 1.11) and 0.72 0.66 0.71 0.68 1.02 (median 0.71), so no single run's median holds the next one within the 20 percent tolerance. The baseline is the median of all ten rounds, 0.857, and the memory tolerance is 0.35, as hello's RAM on the Windows arm64 runner already has; it covers 0.56 to 1.16. Timing is kept.
